quote: Heraclitus said, “All is fire.” Thales said, “All is water.” Pythagoras said, “All is number.”
content: The scoreboard is a joke, but it is a joke with a history in it, and the history is wrong. There is no evidence that Pythagoras said anything about number; the doctrine that “things are numbers” is attributed by Aristotle to “the so-called Pythagoreans” of the fifth century, and Burkert’s Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (1972, a book with no DOI) showed that the mathematical Pythagoras is a construction of the later Platonist tradition, a conclusion Zhmud has qualified but not reversed. “All is water” is Aristotle’s reconstruction of Thales from a single sentence, and “all is fire” compresses Heraclitus’s fragments, in which fire is the medium of exchange for a logos, not a claim that the world is made of fire. What the essay awards Pythagoras a point for is closer to Plato’s Timaeus, in which the elements are geometrical solids, which is why the essay later imagines proteins “lining up in a perfect icosahedron.” None of this changes the essay’s argument, but the essay is making a point about the history of the idea that reality is mathematical, and it gets the history from a slogan.

quote: We know every fundamental physical law that is relevant to a chain of amino acids folding itself into a protein. But we still can’t predict the shape of the protein from the amino acids.
content: Thirteen years later, protein structure prediction was solved to near-experimental accuracy, and the way it was solved contradicts the essay’s next move. AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al. (2021)) does not use the Schrödinger equation or any physics to speak of; it learns from evolutionary covariation in sequence families and from the statistics of the protein structures in the database, which is to say from surface-level regularities of exactly the kind the essay says no longer exist to be found: “we can guess that we won’t find any additional secret patterns that will make biology as easy as a sequence of cubes.” The secret pattern was that evolution has explored a small universe of folds and that residues in contact coevolve (Marks et al. (2011)). The essay was right that logical uncertainty, not ignorance of physics, was the obstacle, and wrong that knowing the master order tells you that “the game is hard” at every level above it; the game turned out to be easy at a level the essay had ruled out. Knowing the fundamental laws told the field nothing about where the tractable structure was, which is the general point Anderson made about “More Is Different” and the essay does not consider.

quote: It’s a good bet that “uncertainty about initial conditions at the boundary” is really indexical uncertainty.
content: This sentence converts ordinary empirical uncertainty into a metaphysical thesis. Uncertainty about the tiger’s location is uncertainty about which way the world is; calling it “indexical” (which cube am I on?) presupposes that every alternative is realized somewhere, in a spatially infinite universe, an inflationary multiverse or an Everett branch, so that the only question is where in the ensemble one sits. That presupposition is a contested cosmological and interpretive claim, argued for in this book only in the quantum sequence and there only for one of the three ensembles. Even granting the ensembles, anthropic reasoning about one’s location does not yet have a settled theory: Bostrom’s book, which the essay cites, ends with two candidate assumptions (self-sampling and self-indication) that give contradictory answers to the same problems, one yielding the Doomsday argument and the other the presumptuous philosopher (Bostrom & Ćirković (2003)), and the subsequent literature has not chosen between them. So the third source of uncertainty, which the essay says is “the most difficult to understand,” is not a resolved category into which the messy tiger can be filed; it is an open problem, and filing the tiger there makes the tiger harder to think about, not easier.

quote: The best current knowledge says that the “real world” is a perfectly regular, deterministic, and very large mathematical object which is highly expensive to simulate.
content: Three claims are bundled here and none of them is “best current knowledge.” Determinism holds only under the Everett or Bohm readings of quantum mechanics; under the textbook interpretation and under objective-collapse theories, which remain live (Bassi et al. (2013)), the world is indeterministic, and the essay is asserting the conclusion of the Many Worlds sequence forty essays before it argues for it. That the world is a mathematical object, rather than being described by one, is Tegmark’s mathematical universe hypothesis (Tegmark (2008)), a minority metaphysical position with known difficulties (most mathematical structures are uncomputable; the hypothesis has no way to say which structure we are in without smuggling in the physics it was meant to replace). And “uncertainty exists in the map, not in the territory” is not a finding but the definition of the essay’s position; on the alternatives just listed, probability is in the territory, which is why the essay Probability Is in the Mind, later in this book, has to argue for the point rather than cite it. The essay’s “three sources of uncertainty” omit a fourth on any of these alternatives, objective chance, and the omission is what allows the conclusion that “the messiness is only in the eye of the beholder.”
